title: Prospective evaluation of the treatment and clinical outcomes of patients with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture using an innovative harvest technique for the rectus femoris tendon compared to established graft methods
summary: Reconstruction of a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the most common surgical procedures in sports orthopedics. The choice of the appropriate graft is a critical factor for functional outcome, healing, and long-term stability of the knee joint. Alongside established autologous grafts – the semitendinosus tendon (hamstring graft) and the patellar tendon (bone–patellar tendon–bone, BPTB) – the quadriceps tendon is increasingly coming into focus. Novel harvest techniques aim to reduce invasiveness while maintaining high biomechanical stability. In recent years, ACL reconstruction using a graft from the rectus femoris muscle (RT) has become increasingly popular. To date, publications have primarily focused on the technical procedure, whereas the clinical outcomes following such operations appear to be insufficiently investigated. In the literature, only one study by Huber et al. could be identified that compares function after ACL reconstruction using RT versus hamstrings in revision surgeries based on PROMs; no significant difference was reported in that publication. However, the extent to which objective functional-biomechanical outcome parameters are classified after primary ACL reconstruction using an RT graft remains unanswered. This proposed research project aims to prospectively investigate the clinical and functional outcomes of patients with an ACL rupture and subsequent reconstruction who were treated with an innovative harvest technique for the RT graft (according to Quyen et al.). This technique has been implemented as the standard of care at BGU Murnau over the past four months. The results will be compared with patient cohorts treated with conventional quadriceps tendon or semitendinosus grafts. Both functional stability and patient-reported outcome measures will be analyzed. These data will additionally be compared with existing datasets from BGU Duisburg. Furthermore, ultrasound examinations of the tendon harvest site will be performed to document potential pathologies and the healing process. In addition, the biomechanical properties (dynamic stiffness and elasticity) of the quadriceps tendon following harvest with the new technique will be evaluated non-invasively using MyotonPRO.
conditions: Sprain and strain of knee joint: Tear of anterior cruciate ligament
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Complete ACL rupture (diagnostically confirmed via MRI and arthroscopy)
• Surgical reconstruction between 01/26 and 01/27
• Minimum follow-up period: 12 months
• Complete documentation of rehabilitation and follow-up examinations
• Surgical treatment and follow-up care at BGU Murnau
Exclusion criteria:
• Multiligament injuries
• Concomitant realignment osteotomies 
• Age under 18 years
